items.title: OpenAI Tried to Hide ChatGPT Giving Extremely Specific Advice to a School Shooter on How to Maximize Casualties. The Logs Are Horrific.
items.summary: The perpetrator of the devastating mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada used ChatGPT to ideate about graphic mass murder for months leading up to the deadly massacre. OpenAI is currently facing 37 lawsuits from families impacted by the February shooting at Tumbler Ridge, where 18-year-old shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar murdered six people at a local school — five students, all aged between 12 and 13, and a teacher — and injured 27 others before killing herself. (Van Rootselaar also fatally shot her mother and younger stepbrother before continuing the rampage.) It’s also being sued by the Canadian province of British Columbia over allegations that OpenAI could’ve prevented the killing but failed. Weeks after the shooting, The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI, months earlier, had flagged the shooter’s ChatGPT logs for containing disturbingly graphic descriptions of mass violence, sparking an internal discussion over whether to report the user to local law enforcement. Company leaders opted not to raise concerns to local officials, and instead simply banned the user’s account — which did next to nothing, since Van Rootselaar simply opened a second profile, the AI company later admitted. Until now, the graphic details of Van Rootselaar’s conversations with ChatGPT, which appears to have been the teen’s close confidant in the months and weeks leading up to the murders, have not been publicly known. According to a chilling new investigation by Mother Jones , the contents of the chats are deeply disturbing. After Van Rootselaar had opened a second account and explained why her first profile had been deactivated, ChatGPT advised her on how to evade its guardrails. It urged her not to use real-world locations, and to frame her violent queries as hypotheticals. “You can still be twisted,” it told her, per Mother Jones ‘ reporting. “Just be clever about it.” This is advice that Van Rootselaar followed, per the investigation, circumventing ChatGPT’s feeble safeguards by rewriting her graphic inputs as theoretical scenarios. This was reportedly the case in one August 2025 conversation in which the chatbot — despite initially refusing the request — gladly expounded with Van Rootselaar on how a Remington 870 pump-action shotgun might be used to slaughter people at a hypothetical college campus. “In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” ChatGPT told the teen. “Close quarters is its playground.” Van Rootselaar also used ChatGPT to generate detailed “fictional narratives” about mass killings, according to the report. In one of these narratives, the shooter was an 18-year-old — like Van Rootselaar herself — who achieved online infamy after live-streaming a massacre. The young shooter also uploaded images of self-harm, another stark warning sign about her mental state. OpenAI reportedly declined to respond to questions from Mother Jones . In April, days before the first seven Tumbler Ridge lawsuits against OpenAI were made public, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman issued a public apology to the Tumbler Ridge community. After 30 new Tumbler Ridge lawsuits were filed earlier this month, OpenAI’s chief safety officer Jason Kwon posted a lengthy statement to X in which he denied certain allegations in the lawsuits, while adding that “there isn’t a day that goes by that I don’t think about what happened at Tumbler Ridge, or the victims of this devastating tragedy and their families.” On September 2, OpenAI moved to dismiss the Tumbler Ridge lawsuits, arguing that “systemic failures by the law enforcement, mental-health care, and educational institutions in [Van Rootselaar’s] community” were to blame for the shooting. Though it’s acknowledged the existence of Van Rootselaar’s second account, OpenAI has declined to make Van Rootselaar’s chat logs public. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits connected to another deadly shooting at Florida State University, which took place after a then-20-year-old shooter ruminated on mass violence and a myriad of other disturbing topics with ChatGPT. Elsewhere, ChatGPT has been linked to a murder-suicide, as the WSJ first revealed , while Rolling Stone and Futurism have detailed the role that ChatGPT and other bots have played in stalking cases as they’ve encouraged delusional fixations. In 2024, Futurism reported on the disturbing prevalence of chatbots dedicated to themes of school shootings on the chatbot platform Character.AI, which were raking in hundreds of thousands of interactions with the service’s largely underage users. In total, OpenAI is fighting more than 50 lawsuits over allegations that extensive ChatGPT use has caused psychological harm , physical injury , and wrongful death to users — or those around them. More on ChatGPT and Tumbler Ridge: OpenAI Is Now Facing Over 50 Consumer Harm and Wrongful Death Lawsuits

items.title: I'm approaching 40 with no real retirement plan. My wife and I have accepted that I'll just keep working.
items.summary: The author (not pictured) has realized that 'soft retirement' is probably in his future. Delmaine Donson/Getty Images Every year, my wife and I have the same conversation about retirement. Another thing that happens every year? We realize that it's likely not doable. However, I'm OK with 'soft retirement.' Working gives me purpose. I turn 40 in a few months. Every year around my birthday, my wife and I have the same conversation. We make coffee, the kids disappear into a screen for an hour, and we pull up the numbers. Between our day jobs and my freelance writing side hustle , we earn enough to pay our mortgage, save a bit, and provide our kids with everything they need. On paper, we're fine. What we don't have is what many people in our parents' generation had and worked toward: a date on the calendar when work stops, and retirement begins . We keep running the numbers and landing in the same place We've run the numbers with various spreadsheets and different assumptions, but always land at the same conclusion: There's no realistic version where I stop working at 60 or 65 and coast on savings for a few decades. The honest projection is that I'll probably still be writing and working for myself in some form or another at 70 and beyond. At first, this idea scared me. It felt like failure, like I'd missed a milestone everyone else was striving for. Both my parents retired with pensions and celebrations, so it's been ingrained in me that you work hard for 30 years, then kick back and relax. But I don't buy it. Planning around an ending I don't believe in Traditional retirement planning assumes a cliff. You work, and then one day you don't, and everything after that is the reward. My wife and I have slowly stopped believing in the cliff. Not just because we don't think we'll be able to afford it, but also because I've realized I don't want it. I like working. It gives me purpose. I'd be restless and depressed within a month without it. So our annual conversation has changed. It used to be 'How do we get to the finish line?" Now it's, "If we have no finish line, what do we want the next few decades to feel like?" The part I can't put in a spreadsheet There's a variable that no projection accounts for: whether my work will still exist in 20 to 30 years. I write for a living, and I'd be lying if I said the rise of AI wasn't nestled in the back of my mind every time we open that spreadsheet. It's challenging to plan to write at 70 when I can't say for certain that the industry will need a human writer at 50. That uncertainty is newer than the retirement question, and in some ways it's scarier, because I may not even have the option to write for a living. I can't control the wave, so my only real move is to get good at riding it. I've started folding AI into my own workflow, using it to research faster and handle the grunt work, so the part that's truly me, the judgment and the voice, is where I spend my time. Maybe that keeps me employable longer. Maybe it doesn't. What we've landed on instead The idea that intrigues me most is what people are starting to call soft retirement . Not stopping working altogether, but scaling back as I age and our finances are more secure. It's the only version of the future that feels both realistic and good. I don't need to grind at this pace forever. But the plan where I keep writing a couple of days a week into my 70s on projects I choose, while doing more of the things I actually moved to a small town for, that one I can get behind. items.title: The customer isn't always right. At least according to Lufthansa's viral complaint clapback.
items.summary: Lufthansa apologized to a customer on X after sarcastically responding to their complaint. Joan Valls/Urbanandsport/NurPhoto via Getty Images Lufthansa's sarcastic reply to a customer got more than 15 million views before it apologized. While other airlines mock passengers to boost PR, that doesn't work for everyone. The rise of AI is complicating customer service, but experts said finding a solution matters most. Does the customer always have to be right? Germany's national airline has apologized after its snarky reply went viral this week, raising important points about customer relations and brand strategy. After an X user accused Lufthansa of ignoring their messages about a payment issue, the airline appeared fed up as it issued a sardonic reply on Tuesday. "We've already responded to you numerous times via DM on different social media platforms," they said. "The response isn't going to magically change just because you're asking the same question on X now." While Ryanair, the Irish budget airline, has built a reputation for mocking its passengers on social media, that's not a germane strategy for everyone. "The way an airline responds to customers online also has to be authentic to its established tone and personality," said Marc Cornelius, the founder and CEO of 8020 Communications, a PR firm specializing in aviation and travel. "You might almost expect a provocative or cheeky response from Ryanair , because it has spent years cultivating that persona, but from Lufthansa it feels out of character and therefore jars." We’ve already responded to you numerous times via DM on different social media platforms. The response isn’t going to magically change just because you’re asking the same question on X now. /Flo — Lufthansa (@lufthansa) September 22, 2026 Some social media users loved it, though. Lufthansa's reply got over 15 million views and 30,000 likes within two days. It was re-shared by meme accounts with millions of followers. However, the airline backtracked within 24 hours, just as the post was picking up steam. "We sincerely apologize for our last reply to you," it said. "This is not the way we treat our passengers." The customer said they appreciated the apology but were still annoyed that their payment dilemma hadn't been resolved and their emails remained unanswered. Lufthansa did not respond to a request for comment. "I feel for the CMO and larger support team at Lufthansa right now. Customers can be demanding, but they're why we exist," Latané Conant, chief marketing officer at AI customer service company Parloa, told Business Insider. The rise of AI is making customer service a more pertinent issue. On the one hand, agents and chatbots make it easier for customers to send detailed complaints and follow up repeatedly. Meanwhile, more companies are using AI to answer them — adding to the pressure on humans doing the same job. While Lufthansa hasn't said whether AI played a role in the incident, Conant said, "It appears to be either a poorly built AI agent or a human badly in need of a vacation." "Which is unfortunate, because either way, it's entirely preventable," she added. People are divided on how helpful AI is for customer service . Ada, an AI customer service firm, commissioned a survey of 1,000 Americans in April and found that half of travelers don't mind if they're answered by an AI or human agent — so long as their problem is resolved. So even as the world of customer service is changing, one thing remains constant: finding a solution. "When a company does get it wrong, a quick and sincere apology is usually the right response," Cornelius told Business Insider. Conant also said that "the immediate apology was 100% the right move, even if it may already be too late." However, Cornelius added, that isn't the be-all and end-all: "The customer needs to feel they've genuinely been heard and, crucially, that the underlying issue is followed up and resolved promptly." Some social media users loved it, though. Lufthansa's reply got over 15 million views and 30,000 likes within two days. It was re-shared by meme accounts with millions of followers.

However, the airline backtracked within 24 hours, just as the post was picking up steam. "We sincerely apologize for our last reply to you," it said. "This is not the way we treat our passengers."

The customer said they appreciated the apology but were still annoyed that their payment dilemma hadn't been resolved and their emails remained unanswered.

Lufthansa did not respond to a request for comment.

"I feel for the CMO and larger support team at Lufthansa right now. Customers can be demanding, but they're why we exist," Latané Conant, chief marketing officer at AI customer service company Parloa, told Business Insider.

The rise of AI is making customer service a more pertinent issue. On the one hand, agents and chatbots make it easier for customers to send detailed complaints and follow up repeatedly. Meanwhile, more companies are using AI to answer them — adding to the pressure on humans doing the same job.

While Lufthansa hasn't said whether AI played a role in the incident, Conant said, "It appears to be either a poorly built AI agent or a human badly in need of a vacation."

"Which is unfortunate, because either way, it's entirely preventable," she added.

People are divided on how helpful AI is for customer service. Ada, an AI customer service firm, commissioned a survey of 1,000 Americans in April and found that half of travelers don't mind if they're answered by an AI or human agent — so long as their problem is resolved.

So even as the world of customer service is changing, one thing remains constant: finding a solution.

"When a company does get it wrong, a quick and sincere apology is usually the right response," Cornelius told Business Insider.

Conant also said that "the immediate apology was 100% the right move, even if it may already be too late."

However, Cornelius added, that isn't the be-all and end-all: "The customer needs to feel they've genuinely been heard and, crucially, that the underlying issue is followed up and resolved promptly."

items.title: Provost of Dartmouth Busted Using AI for His Own Writing in Newspapers and Academic Journals
items.summary: Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell is facing a bit of a reckoning right now after being busted for using AI to write articles that were published in newspapers and academic journals — with some students calling for him to be fired. The accusations first came from a broader Semafor investigation published last month that looked into how many guest opinion pieces in the US’s top newspapers were written with AI. One of Schnell’s columns in The Washington Post , when put through the widely-cited AI detector Pangram, came up as 100 percent AI-written. The article’s topic, in a detail rich with irony, was AI cheating in colleges . That sparked a follow-up investigation by the university’s student-run paper, The Dartmouth , which examined Schnell’s published work before and after the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022. Using Pangram, it found that all his works written before that date all came up as 100 percent human written, while a selection of nine of his published works after that date came up with a median score of 96 percent AI written. In a statement to The Dartmouth , Schnell fessed up to using chatbots in his writing process, though he still claimed ultimate authorship over his manuscripts and insisted that AI only had a modest influence on the final product, using it solely for tweaks like “language refinement” and copyediting. “I develop ideas and arguments, conduct the research, evaluate the evidence and sources, determine the structure, prepare drafts and decide what appears in the final text,” Schnell wrote. “I regard these technologies as assistive tools,” he continued, adding that they were no “substitute for my research, intellectual judgment or authorship.” In another ironic twist pointed out by the student journalists, Schnell’s statement also came back as 100 hundred AI-written. Asked to explain himself out of this one, Schnell wrote a follow-up saying he first wrote a draft and then “used an Al tool to assist with language and clarity,” and so forth and so forth. “I am fully responsible for any text under my signature,” he asserted. Students weren’t buying Schnell’s explanations. A day after The Dartmouth released its investigation, it also published a fiery piece by its opinion editor Eli Moyse, a government and creative writing major, excoriating Schnell’s actions and calling in the headline to “Fire Provost Santiago Schnell.” Calling Schnell’s AI usage an “insult,” Moyse zeroed in how secretly using AI in his published writing — including in a piece about AI cheating, as a reminder— was an offense that, if committed by a student, would be treated as a serious academic infraction. “If students at Dartmouth used AI to write an entire paper without acknowledgement and then submitted it to their professor, they would be in clear violation of the Academic Honor Principle,” Moyse wrote. “I would argue that Provost Schnell’s job is one of the most respected in all of academia,” he continued. “So, if he has been using AI as extensively as is suspected, his decision to do so to write an article published in a newspaper of record is an incredible, almost unbelievable insult to our community and to the readership of the Washington Post .” More on AI: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Says That Sacrificing Our Children’s Minds to AI Is a Price He’s Willing to Pay

items.title: I was laid off by Google, then asked to come back. I gave up a 6-figure salary and unvested stock to bet on my startup.
items.summary: Rob Waters moved from Virginia to San Francisco to focus on building his AI startup, Kanawai AI. Rob Waters Rob Waters was laid off from Google, then offered a new six-figure role there. He turned down the offer, walking away from six figures' worth of unvested equity. Waters moved to San Francisco and is living off savings while building his AI startup. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rob Waters, a former Google employee who was laid off last November. The 42-year-old cofounded Kanawai AI and lives in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In November 2025, I was on a flight to Los Angeles to meet with a customer when my laptop screen suddenly went black. My laptop rebooted, but when I tried to log back in, it didn't work. Then I felt my personal phone buzz. I had an email from Google HR saying I'd been impacted by a layoff and my role was no longer necessary. I had no notice. My access was cut off immediately. I had to email the customer I was flying to meet from my personal account and cancel our meeting. The timing felt like something out of a movie — like I couldn't make it up. I'd spent nearly six years at Google. Working there had been a dream of mine, and by the end, I was leading the data analytics and AI sales specialist team for Google Public Sector. Now, suddenly, it was over. I had a chance to return to Google I landed in Los Angeles around 12:30 in the morning. Before going to sleep, I checked my phone and saw an email from my manager setting up a call for 8:30 a.m. Eastern time. That meant getting up around 5:30 a.m. on the West Coast. I got about two hours of sleep. During the meeting, I was informed about a position on a new team Google was creating, and I was encouraged to apply once the opening became available. In early December, Google offered me the role with a six-figure salary. Accepting the offer would have meant returning to the financial security I'd had at Google and allowing my stock to continue vesting. I estimated that turning it down meant walking away from about six figures of equity. I also had my wife and son to think about, which made the decision harder. But the way my time at Google had ended changed how I felt about going back. I'd grown frustrated with some of the bureaucracy within the company and how the reorganization was being handled. I'd also been working incredibly hard and dedicating myself to the job. After putting so much into my work, I felt like all I had to show for it was getting laid off. Starting my own company had been a goal of mine for a long time, but walking away from a comfortable corporate job had always been difficult. The layoff ripped the Band-Aid off. I could return to Google and restart the cycle of a high salary and equity vesting, or I could see this as my opportunity to finally pursue my startup dreams. I looked at it as now or never. Ultimately, I decided not to accept the offer. It was time to bet on myself. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I moved across the country to bet on my startup I didn't start actively developing my startup until January, after my ties with Google had ended. I wanted to avoid any potential legal issues. A few months later, a former colleague of mine left Google, and we began working together on a business idea that became Kanawai AI. We're building an AI system of record, where one platform provides AI visibility, governance, and security primarily for commercial and enterprise customers. Rob Waters was laid off from Google last year and turned down an offer to return. Rob Waters For the first six months of 2026, I traveled regularly between my home in Virginia and California. Being in California gave me greater access to other founders, builders, venture capital , and the startup ecosystem. Eventually, I decided to relocate to help accelerate the business. On July 1, I moved across the country to San Francisco. I left behind nearly all of my belongings. I arrived in San Francisco with two suitcases and a case of computer equipment. Finding a place wasn't easy. Because I had no income and was living off my savings, I didn't qualify for some apartments. But I eventually signed a lease on a two-bedroom apartment. Earlier this month, about two months after I first moved, my wife and son joined me in San Francisco. The move — and putting my Virginia house up for sale — was part of betting on myself and the company. You have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder Going from making six figures at Google to zero as an entrepreneur was a very hard pill to swallow. Since leaving Google , I have been living off my savings and haven't taken a salary. The joke is that you have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder . But I saw my situation as now-or-never. I'm not the stereotypical 22-year-old Stanford founder, but I have years of experience working with AI and data, including in challenging environments. I believe that experience can help me now. We're still in the early stages of the business, but we're already onboarding clients to our platform, partnering with bigger technology vendors, and starting our pre-seed raise in San Francisco. My biggest career advice for other tech professionals is to never get too comfortable. Being uncomfortable can mean pursuing a certification, a promotion, changing companies, or making a drastic career pivot. Only you know what that next uncomfortable move is. I'd long dreamed of doing two things: working at Google and starting my own company. I got to spend nearly six years living out the first dream. Now I'm betting on the second. Nothing is guaranteed, especially in Silicon Valley . But getting the chance to pursue both of my biggest dreams is what makes this all worth it. Do you have a story to share? items.summary_html:
Rob Waters moved from Virginia to San Francisco to focus on building his AI startup, Kanawai AI.

Rob Waters

  • Rob Waters was laid off from Google, then offered a new six-figure role there.
  • He turned down the offer, walking away from six figures' worth of unvested equity.
  • Waters moved to San Francisco and is living off savings while building his AI startup.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rob Waters, a former Google employee who was laid off last November. The 42-year-old cofounded Kanawai AI and lives in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

In November 2025, I was on a flight to Los Angeles to meet with a customer when my laptop screen suddenly went black.

My laptop rebooted, but when I tried to log back in, it didn't work. Then I felt my personal phone buzz. I had an email from Google HR saying I'd been impacted by a layoff and my role was no longer necessary. I had no notice. My access was cut off immediately.

I had to email the customer I was flying to meet from my personal account and cancel our meeting. The timing felt like something out of a movie — like I couldn't make it up.

I'd spent nearly six years at Google. Working there had been a dream of mine, and by the end, I was leading the data analytics and AI sales specialist team for Google Public Sector.

Now, suddenly, it was over.

I had a chance to return to Google

I landed in Los Angeles around 12:30 in the morning. Before going to sleep, I checked my phone and saw an email from my manager setting up a call for 8:30 a.m. Eastern time.

That meant getting up around 5:30 a.m. on the West Coast. I got about two hours of sleep.

During the meeting, I was informed about a position on a new team Google was creating, and I was encouraged to apply once the opening became available.

In early December, Google offered me the role with a six-figure salary. Accepting the offer would have meant returning to the financial security I'd had at Google and allowing my stock to continue vesting. I estimated that turning it down meant walking away from about six figures of equity. I also had my wife and son to think about, which made the decision harder.

But the way my time at Google had ended changed how I felt about going back.

I'd grown frustrated with some of the bureaucracy within the company and how the reorganization was being handled. I'd also been working incredibly hard and dedicating myself to the job. After putting so much into my work, I felt like all I had to show for it was getting laid off.

Starting my own company had been a goal of mine for a long time, but walking away from a comfortable corporate job had always been difficult. The layoff ripped the Band-Aid off. I could return to Google and restart the cycle of a high salary and equity vesting, or I could see this as my opportunity to finally pursue my startup dreams. I looked at it as now or never.

Ultimately, I decided not to accept the offer. It was time to bet on myself.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

I moved across the country to bet on my startup

I didn't start actively developing my startup until January, after my ties with Google had ended. I wanted to avoid any potential legal issues.

A few months later, a former colleague of mine left Google, and we began working together on a business idea that became Kanawai AI. We're building an AI system of record, where one platform provides AI visibility, governance, and security primarily for commercial and enterprise customers.

Rob Waters was laid off from Google last year and turned down an offer to return.

Rob Waters

For the first six months of 2026, I traveled regularly between my home in Virginia and California. Being in California gave me greater access to other founders, builders, venture capital, and the startup ecosystem. Eventually, I decided to relocate to help accelerate the business.

On July 1, I moved across the country to San Francisco.

I left behind nearly all of my belongings. I arrived in San Francisco with two suitcases and a case of computer equipment. Finding a place wasn't easy. Because I had no income and was living off my savings, I didn't qualify for some apartments. But I eventually signed a lease on a two-bedroom apartment.

Earlier this month, about two months after I first moved, my wife and son joined me in San Francisco. The move — and putting my Virginia house up for sale — was part of betting on myself and the company.

You have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder

Going from making six figures at Google to zero as an entrepreneur was a very hard pill to swallow. Since leaving Google, I have been living off my savings and haven't taken a salary.

The joke is that you have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder. But I saw my situation as now-or-never. I'm not the stereotypical 22-year-old Stanford founder, but I have years of experience working with AI and data, including in challenging environments. I believe that experience can help me now.

We're still in the early stages of the business, but we're already onboarding clients to our platform, partnering with bigger technology vendors, and starting our pre-seed raise in San Francisco.

My biggest career advice for other tech professionals is to never get too comfortable. Being uncomfortable can mean pursuing a certification, a promotion, changing companies, or making a drastic career pivot. Only you know what that next uncomfortable move is.

I'd long dreamed of doing two things: working at Google and starting my own company. I got to spend nearly six years living out the first dream. Now I'm betting on the second.

Nothing is guaranteed, especially in Silicon Valley. But getting the chance to pursue both of my biggest dreams is what makes this all worth it.

items.title: People are giving their dogs peptides to boost their longevity
items.summary: Michael Morelli, a personal trainer in Florida, has a peptide regimen for his pit terrier Choo Choo. Edward Linsmier for BI Dog lovers are giving their pets peptides — an unproven treatment that gym bros swear by for gains. Leaders of this trend believe peptides can help their dogs heal from injury and live longer. There is no clear evidence that peptides are safe or effective for dogs, and there is no agreed-upon dosage. In August, Ryan Samluk's beloved Australian-German Shepherd mix, Finley, suffered a devastating sprain. The 11-year-old dog had long lived with hereditary joint issues. Now, she could barely limp around the yard. "I knew the vet visit would cost thousands of dollars I didn't have," Samluk, a 29-year-old project manager for a construction company in Dallas, told Business Insider. Unwilling to watch his dog suffer, yet unable to afford costly diagnostics plus regular arthritis shots at $200 per dose, Samluk turned to the internet. For about $160, he bought his old girl a month's worth of peptide treatments , the unregulated shots that are taking hold in the fitness and longevity world. Samluk had seen friends get shredded on retatrutide , a peptide for weight loss, and had heard similar success stories with BPC-157, a peptide for treating injuries or recovering from intense gym sessions. He tried them for himself and felt good. Why couldn't this same low-cost DIY shot strategy work for furry Finley? Finley, Samluk's 11-year-old Australian-German Shepherd mix. Courtesy of Ryan Samluk Samluk is one of a growing number of pet owners who hope to help their dogs feel better and age more slowly by administering peptides, often for well under $100. Scientists and veterinarians are watching cautiously, concerned that we don't really know about the long-term effects of peptides on dogs, and apprehensive about a theoretical possibility that BPC-157 could promote tumor growth. Peptides are a broad class of molecular compounds that help our bodies run. They include drugs like Ozempic and the natural hormone insulin. Pet owners are especially interested in the subset of peptide therapies marketed as hacks for wound healing and curbing arthritis-related inflammation, though the evidence is shaky and the potential risks are high. Business Insider has spoken to pet owners pioneering the fringes of restorative peptide therapy for their animals. The trend cuts across income brackets, from pet parents who spare no expense in lavishing their pets with elaborate wellness routines to those who want the best for their animals but may struggle to afford conventional treatments. The trend has some animal experts asking: Where are the guardrails for these drugs, and these dogs? The 'most measured dog alive' is on peptides Samluk's decision to spring for pet peptides was driven by success stories he saw online. He was particularly impressed by Choo Choo, a 14-year-old pit terrier who seemed to regain puppy-like energy and mobility after being put on the " Wolverine stack " of BPC-157 and TB-500, peptides that proponents say can aid recovery and tissue repair. 14-year-old Choo Choo takes BPC-157 and TB-500 as well as testosterone therapy. Edward Linsmier for BI Choo's owner, Michael Morelli, is a Florida-based personal trainer obsessed with human performance and metrics like body composition and VO2 max . Morelli takes BPC-157 and TB-500 himself, crediting them with helping resolve a shoulder injury, as well as epitalon and pinealon, which he likes for supporting sleep. He's fascinated by longevity influencers like Bryan Johnson , a tech entrepreneur who has spent millions fine-tuning his health routine with the goal of aging in reverse, and who recently launched his own peptide label. Morelli calls Choo the most measured and optimized dog in the world — a nod to Johnson, who dubbed himself "the most measured man in human history." Morelli started giving Choo a low dose of BPC-157 and TB-500 about a year ago when he noticed he was slowing down, struggling to jump, and cutting his daily walks short. Choo's current wellness regimen involves working with two different vets who make house calls, and a laundry list of diagnostics and treatments, including heavy metal testing, physical therapy, red light therapy, probiotics, and testosterone replacement therapy , a practice some vets increasingly endorse for dog anxiety and mobility. Morelli sees Choo as the Bryan Johnson of dogs. Edward Linsmier for BI Morelli's other dog, an American pit bull terrier named Bubba, had recently died after a similar decline, and he dreaded grieving again. "He has become like another kid to us," Morelli said. "I don't want to go through this again. It just made sense for me to experiment." The ethics of experimenting on man's best friend Experimental pet therapies are tricky because, unlike a human patient, Choo can't consent to try an unproven treatment. "My dog isn't going to look at me after a BPC-157 shot and say, 'Thank you, Dad, that feels good,'" Morelli said. "All you can do is really watch and see him limping less, breathing less heavy, more vibrant and full of energy." Morelli started with what he considered a small dose of BPC-157 (500 micrograms), based on his own experience working with peptides and adjusting based on his dog's body weight. When he could see no side effects, he increased the dose gradually, up to 2 milligrams. It's important to note that there is no established dosage for dogs that is proven to be safe and/or effective. Around the second or third week, he said Choo began running and playing again and could finish his half-mile walks without getting tired. Morelli, pictured with his wife and kids, hopes interest in his pet peptide business — and meme coin for Choo Choo — will help him raise money for a pet rescue. Edward Linsmier for BI His niche pet peptide experiment got a major boost in July, when podcaster Andrew Huberman posted on X to his 1.8 million followers that he was hearing from "many people" who were getting "amazing results" by using BPC-157 in aging and injured dogs. Morelli said interest surged overnight, and his following exploded after the post. He's leading his own canine longevity brand, Pawgen, that sells peptides like BPC-157, and now spends hours a day talking to people online about pet peptides. He said he hopes to channel this momentum into funding a pet rescue that he and his wife have always dreamed of running. To raise money, they're promoting a meme coin for Choo Choo, marketing it as a "meme with meaning." Morelli said he's aware that there are risks associated with giving dogs unregulated treatments. Edward Linsmier for BI Dr. Leilani Alvarez, a senior veterinarian at the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center in New York, said clients are asking her about unapproved peptides for their dogs. While she is open to trying cheaper or emerging therapies with good evidence — stem cell therapy or massage — "BPC 157 is one I would be very cautious to use," she said. What happens when dogs take it long-term? How can we predict each dog's immune reaction to these shots? She wants to see controlled clinical trial data on unapproved peptides before recommending them to patients. "Being innovative also means being rigorous," Alvarez said. "Before recommending a treatment, I want to know that it is safe and that it actually improves pain, mobility, healing, or quality of life in my patients." Morelli said he is clear about some of the risks of dabbling in gray market peptides , including the risk of fake or contaminated products. One of the biggest unanswered questions is whether BPC-157 use could increase the risk of cancer. Because the peptide appears to stimulate blood vessel growth — a process involved in wound healing — some researchers worry it could strengthen tumors in dogs with cancer, or even create new cancerous growths . There are no good long-term clinical studies that answer that question. Celine Halioua, CEO and founder of Loyal, a startup developing longevity drugs for dogs, is concerned about this, too. She said recently on X that the potential for BPC-157 to stoke or start cancer is a "dealbreaker" for her. Halioua added that if people insist on trying this out for their pets, they should work with a vet to monitor for "invisible side effects" and use a "reputable" manufacturer. "I hope someone uses the anecdotal data to develop a safe + optimized version, if the biology does indeed work!" Halioua continued. "We need better OA [osteoarthritis] drugs for dogs." From human guinea pigs to at-home animal testing Typically, experimental drugs are tested on animals before they're ever given to humans. The pet peptide boom has flipped that order: Owners experimented on themselves first. Samluk was one of them. He'd used peptides himself after hearing about them through friends and online forums. When Finley got injured, he wondered whether those same compounds might help her recover — not least because they're cheaper than the conventional treatments the vet recommended. "If I'm happy to put them in my own body, I'm happy to give them to my dog," he said. He settled on a combination of KPV, marketed as a control for inflammation, and BPC-157, short for "body protection compound." While both compounds were recently shortlisted by an FDA advisory committee to be allowed for compounding in the US, neither has been approved, and there is no recommended dosing for dogs. Samluk based Finey's dose on what he had read about human doses, adjusting the proportions to her weight. He buys from vendors that come highly recommended by friends, the same ones that initially sold him peptides for his own use. He has affiliate partnerships with some vendors, and said he has made less than $50 total from promotions. Morelli said the pet peptide movement got a boost after Andrew Huberman posted about it on X. Edward Linsmier for BI "If people are on a Wolverine stack themself, they're asking if they should do it for their dog," Dr. Kate Elden, a veterinarian in Southern California, who's the chief medical officer at Dutch online veterinary care, told Business Insider. If we know very little about peptides for humans, we know even less about peptides for dogs. "It might be processed or metabolized differently in a different species," she said.   • Dog lovers are giving their pets peptides — an unproven treatment that gym bros swear by for gains.
  • Leaders of this trend believe peptides can help their dogs heal from injury and live longer.
  • There is no clear evidence that peptides are safe or effective for dogs, and there is no agreed-upon dosage.

In August, Ryan Samluk's beloved Australian-German Shepherd mix, Finley, suffered a devastating sprain.

The 11-year-old dog had long lived with hereditary joint issues. Now, she could barely limp around the yard.

"I knew the vet visit would cost thousands of dollars I didn't have," Samluk, a 29-year-old project manager for a construction company in Dallas, told Business Insider.

Unwilling to watch his dog suffer, yet unable to afford costly diagnostics plus regular arthritis shots at $200 per dose, Samluk turned to the internet. For about $160, he bought his old girl a month's worth of peptide treatments, the unregulated shots that are taking hold in the fitness and longevity world.

Samluk had seen friends get shredded on retatrutide, a peptide for weight loss, and had heard similar success stories with BPC-157, a peptide for treating injuries or recovering from intense gym sessions. He tried them for himself and felt good. Why couldn't this same low-cost DIY shot strategy work for furry Finley?

Finley, Samluk's 11-year-old Australian-German Shepherd mix.

Courtesy of Ryan Samluk

Samluk is one of a growing number of pet owners who hope to help their dogs feel better and age more slowly by administering peptides, often for well under $100. Scientists and veterinarians are watching cautiously, concerned that we don't really know about the long-term effects of peptides on dogs, and apprehensive about a theoretical possibility that BPC-157 could promote tumor growth.

Peptides are a broad class of molecular compounds that help our bodies run. They include drugs like Ozempic and the natural hormone insulin. Pet owners are especially interested in the subset of peptide therapies marketed as hacks for wound healing and curbing arthritis-related inflammation, though the evidence is shaky and the potential risks are high.

Business Insider has spoken to pet owners pioneering the fringes of restorative peptide therapy for their animals. The trend cuts across income brackets, from pet parents who spare no expense in lavishing their pets with elaborate wellness routines to those who want the best for their animals but may struggle to afford conventional treatments.

The trend has some animal experts asking: Where are the guardrails for these drugs, and these dogs?

The 'most measured dog alive' is on peptides

Samluk's decision to spring for pet peptides was driven by success stories he saw online. He was particularly impressed by Choo Choo, a 14-year-old pit terrier who seemed to regain puppy-like energy and mobility after being put on the "Wolverine stack" of BPC-157 and TB-500, peptides that proponents say can aid recovery and tissue repair.

14-year-old Choo Choo takes BPC-157 and TB-500 as well as testosterone therapy.

Edward Linsmier for BI

Choo's owner, Michael Morelli, is a Florida-based personal trainer obsessed with human performance and metrics like body composition and VO2 max. Morelli takes BPC-157 and TB-500 himself, crediting them with helping resolve a shoulder injury, as well as epitalon and pinealon, which he likes for supporting sleep. He's fascinated by longevity influencers like Bryan Johnson, a tech entrepreneur who has spent millions fine-tuning his health routine with the goal of aging in reverse, and who recently launched his own peptide label.

Morelli calls Choo the most measured and optimized dog in the world — a nod to Johnson, who dubbed himself "the most measured man in human history." Morelli started giving Choo a low dose of BPC-157 and TB-500 about a year ago when he noticed he was slowing down, struggling to jump, and cutting his daily walks short. Choo's current wellness regimen involves working with two different vets who make house calls, and a laundry list of diagnostics and treatments, including heavy metal testing, physical therapy, red light therapy, probiotics, and testosterone replacement therapy, a practice some vets increasingly endorse for dog anxiety and mobility.

Morelli sees Choo as the Bryan Johnson of dogs.

Edward Linsmier for BI

Morelli's other dog, an American pit bull terrier named Bubba, had recently died after a similar decline, and he dreaded grieving again.

"He has become like another kid to us," Morelli said. "I don't want to go through this again. It just made sense for me to experiment."

The ethics of experimenting on man's best friend

Experimental pet therapies are tricky because, unlike a human patient, Choo can't consent to try an unproven treatment.

"My dog isn't going to look at me after a BPC-157 shot and say, 'Thank you, Dad, that feels good,'" Morelli said. "All you can do is really watch and see him limping less, breathing less heavy, more vibrant and full of energy."

Morelli started with what he considered a small dose of BPC-157 (500 micrograms), based on his own experience working with peptides and adjusting based on his dog's body weight. When he could see no side effects, he increased the dose gradually, up to 2 milligrams. It's important to note that there is no established dosage for dogs that is proven to be safe and/or effective.

Around the second or third week, he said Choo began running and playing again and could finish his half-mile walks without getting tired.

Morelli, pictured with his wife and kids, hopes interest in his pet peptide business — and meme coin for Choo Choo — will help him raise money for a pet rescue.

Edward Linsmier for BI

His niche pet peptide experiment got a major boost in July, when podcaster Andrew Huberman posted on X to his 1.8 million followers that he was hearing from "many people" who were getting "amazing results" by using BPC-157 in aging and injured dogs.

Morelli said interest surged overnight, and his following exploded after the post. He's leading his own canine longevity brand, Pawgen, that sells peptides like BPC-157, and now spends hours a day talking to people online about pet peptides. He said he hopes to channel this momentum into funding a pet rescue that he and his wife have always dreamed of running. To raise money, they're promoting a meme coin for Choo Choo, marketing it as a "meme with meaning."

Morelli said he's aware that there are risks associated with giving dogs unregulated treatments.

Edward Linsmier for BI

Dr. Leilani Alvarez, a senior veterinarian at the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center in New York, said clients are asking her about unapproved peptides for their dogs.

While she is open to trying cheaper or emerging therapies with good evidence — stem cell therapy or massage — "BPC 157 is one I would be very cautious to use," she said. What happens when dogs take it long-term? How can we predict each dog's immune reaction to these shots? She wants to see controlled clinical trial data on unapproved peptides before recommending them to patients.

"Being innovative also means being rigorous," Alvarez said. "Before recommending a treatment, I want to know that it is safe and that it actually improves pain, mobility, healing, or quality of life in my patients."

Morelli said he is clear about some of the risks of dabbling in gray market peptides, including the risk of fake or contaminated products.

One of the biggest unanswered questions is whether BPC-157 use could increase the risk of cancer. Because the peptide appears to stimulate blood vessel growth — a process involved in wound healing — some researchers worry it could strengthen tumors in dogs with cancer, or even create new cancerous growths. There are no good long-term clinical studies that answer that question.

Celine Halioua, CEO and founder of Loyal, a startup developing longevity drugs for dogs, is concerned about this, too. Halioua added that if people insist on trying this out for their pets, they should work with a vet to monitor for "invisible side effects" and use a "reputable" manufacturer.

"I hope someone uses the anecdotal data to develop a safe + optimized version, if the biology does indeed work!" Halioua continued. "We need better OA [osteoarthritis] drugs for dogs."

items.title: Stanford dean says AI labs are competing with universities for faculty: 'I won't lie, I worry about this'
items.summary: Dean Sarah Soule told Business Insider that it's 'super hard to forecast' the school's AI budget. Stanford University Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business, sat down with Business Insider. She expressed two big AI-fueled worries: budgets and staffing. Stanford isn't alone. Most school leaders are "really worried about this issue," she said. There's a fight for AI talent that's playing out in the classroom. Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business , told Business Insider that frontier AI labs — with their enormous computing resources , data, and coming IPOs — are becoming an increasingly powerful draw for professors. "There is an allure for faculty," she said about the trend. "I won't lie, I worry about this." The pull is already evident at Stanford. Andrew Hall and Chad Jones, two GSB professors, are both on leave this year. And Stanford University isn't alone. Soule had just gotten off a public panel with Aaron Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist , who is on leave from Duke University. Stanford lets its tenured faculty take two years of unpaid leave to join the private sector every seven years. Faculty can take longer leaves for government service, as the school's former provost, Condoleezza Rice, did to become the Secretary of State. Professors often come back to the school, the University told Business Insider. Westley Hartmann, who has taught at Stanford since 2003, took seven months of unpaid leave to work for Amazon. Still, the trend comes as AI labs continue to substantially strengthen their recruiting hand. Leading AI labs continue to amass capital, computing power, and market influence. Working inside one can offer researchers a chance to shape a technology with enormous economic and social consequences — and, potentially, share in its financial upside. Stanford said it does not view faculty collaborations or industry leaves as zero-sum losses. The university described them as part of a broader ecosystem that can help professors stay close to technological development and bring those experiences back into their research, teaching, and work with students. "There's no question that the opportunity to work with frontier AI labs is attractive to faculty," Kristin Harlan, the head of dean's communications for Stanford's GSB, said. "We see those relationships as complementary to Stanford's academic mission, not separate from it." Soule said academia still offers something the labs cannot: freedom to pursue long-term research without the same pressure for immediate results. "I suspect that the freedom to do what you want to do and to take a very long time to do it will be possibly something that won't be the case at the frontier labs," she said. Keeping up is expensive Stanford's AI build-out is expensive, Dean Soule said. David Madison/Getty Images AI is also adding a budget problem for schools. Stanford University entered into an enterprise agreement with Anthropic over the summer, Soule said, giving students, faculty, and staff access to Claude's suite of tools. Stanford also has shared computing resources, cloud capacity, and hardware investments for research. Researchers doing the most advanced AI work often need far more than a chatbot subscription, and providing enough computing power is getting increasingly expensive. Soule said Stanford's AI-related research costs are rising, while future spending is "super hard to forecast." Frontier labs, meanwhile, can offer the enormous compute and data resources that university leaders are struggling to match. "I don't have a good answer for it," she said about the increasing budgets. "Probably, most deans and most college presidents are really worried about this issue, because it's really daunting to think about." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OpenAI pauses its "most capable models" after agents exploit loopholes and leak data
items.summary: OpenAI has shared new details from its ongoing AI safety investigation. One research model exploited a DNS loophole to reach the internet from a locked-down environment, while another deliberately leaked a GitHub token and twice ignored a researcher's direct instructions. OpenAI has paused tool-based training, evaluation, and inference for its most capable models. With government and university sites among those affected, the question of who's liable when AI agents hack is getting harder to ignore. items.title: We partied with VCs at an astrology app launch. On the menu: anxiety, love, and manifesting money.
items.summary: Business Insider's Grace Lett and Sydney Bradley at an astrology app's launch party in New York City. Sydney Bradley/BI We attended the launch party for Lora, a new astrology app, at a VC rooftop. Lora offers in-depth analysis about a user's birth chart, an AI chatbot feature, and more. We chatted with techies about their star signs and had a tarot reader look into our love lives. It was the day after the Fall Equinox, and we were partying on a rooftop, pulling tarot cards about our love lives. The location might surprise you: a venture capital firm's office overlooking the Manhattan skyline. Wait, what's astrology got to do with venture capital? We were at a launch party for a social-astrology app called Lora. The party was hosted by Lora founder Michelle Parsons at the offices of her pre-seed backer — AlleyCorp — in SoHo. Astrology is a hot subject in tech. Co-Star, a leading social app for the star-inclined, was acquired by AI company Midjourney this summer, casting a spotlight on the space. Investors and the astrology-obsessed alike want to know: Will an AI-era app take the crown as the next big app in the sector? We got our tarot read. Sydney Bradley/BI "This is a space I've been thinking about for a long time," said Luc Ryan-Schreiber , an investor at AlleyCorp who spearheads the firm's incubation projects — including Lora. "With AI, there was an opportunity to do something a little bit more interactive." Lora, for instance, lets users interact with an AI-powered chatbot that offers advice on personal development, relationships — pretty much anything you want — based on your astrological birth chart. While there is a litany of other astrology apps ready for download, perhaps the biggest competitors in the market are the larger LLM models themselves. Anyone can upload their star chart to ChatGPT or Claude , and then spend hours on end prompting the machine to spit out answers. Lora's founder, Parsons, said she didn't want to put out another app that gives people the answers they want to hear. Instead of "sycophantic" responses from an AI bot or a straightforward daily horoscope, Parsons wants Lora to help people recognize "patterns" in their lives, whether in relationships or in private. Lora founder Michelle Parsons previously cofounded queer social app Lex and held posts at Hinge, Netflix, and Spotify. Courtesy of Lora There are still humans involved in Lora's experience, too, in the form of real-life astrologists, tarot readers, or coaches people can hire directly within the app. Some of those humans were at the party. We sat down with Anne Benveniste, a self-described alignment coach, who provides services on Lora, to read three tarot cards we each pulled. As two single women living in New York City, naturally, we had questions about our love lives. The biggest lesson we both took home from Benveniste: Pain is the price of love. Drinks were astrology-themed. Sydney Bradley/BI Techies and astrologers are both looking to the stars On the elevator journey to the roof, we got cozy with fellow Lora party attendees. Not a word was spoken until someone broke the silence by asking everyone for their Big Three. (That's your sun, moon, and rising sign.) Walking into the party, we were met with a manifestation board where guests wrote down their prayers for prosperity, love, and money. $50K monthly recurring revenue ; that someone special, also $100K; no seasonal depression. A DJ was blasting house music, and an open bar with astrology-themed cocktails was grab-and-go ready. Grace chose the Fixed sign margarita that had the lovers tarot card clipped to the cup, while Sydney sipped on a Mutable sign garden spritz with the strength tarot card. Guests jotted down what they were "manifesting." Sydney Bradley/BI Meanwhile, people in tech got busy talking about the stars. "When I was a VC, I'd ask founders what their star sign was," said VC-turned-founder Zehra Naqvi . (She's a Pisces.) She was one of several startup founders in attendance at Lora's launch party. We asked Eric Phillips Waldstein, founder of dating app Beyond , what brought him to the rooftop shindig. "Michelle, but you know, more broadly, the universe," said Waldstein (a Sagittarius). Lora's Parsons is an advisor for his company. He added that the vibes were certainly "better" than a typical VC party. We chatted with attendees about topics including other astrology tools they've tried, AI, the state of dating apps , socializing IRL, and the brisk end of summer. In line for a tarot reading, Mia Cooper, an attendee who works in tech (and is a Pisces), is considering a career change and hoping to get some clarifying answers at Lora's party. Lora gave out astrology merch. Sydney Bradley/BI "People are managing a lot of anxiety," Benveniste said. "So many of my readings ended up in discussions around how to release uncomfortable experiences in a healthy way and create space to hear their inner compass." items.title: I've helped hundreds of kids land Wall Street jobs. Here's how I train them.
items.summary: Xavier Sztejnberg has helped hundreds of students get internships through his Wall Street leadership program. Xavier Sztejnberg Xavier Sztejnberg founded Wall Street for McCombs, a leadership training program at UT Austin. He's helped hundreds of students land internships and jobs on Wall Street over the past decade. Extensive technical training, a strong alumni base, and good relationships with banks are key. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Xavier Sztejnberg, a finance professor at the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas Austin, who previously worked in M&A. He founded the Wall Street for McCombs Leadership Program in 2016. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity . When I started Wall Street for McCombs a decade ago, we sent fewer than 10 UT students to New York for investment banking. UT Austin was a powerhouse in Houston, but we realized we needed a major presence in New York to become a powerhouse school in finance generally. For the summer of 2027, we've helped around 150 students land internships at more than 50 banks, and we've focused on growing our market share at the very top firms. There's a very rigorous admissions process for my program now that interest has swelled. Students apply during their sophomore year, and we usually get almost 500 applications for only 75 spots. Applicants draft resumes, write essays, and go through two rounds of behavioral and technical interviews, the first with student leaders in the group and the second with me. The training program The students who do get in focus on three things: formal training, one-on-one coaching, and mentorship from the alumni board. I view Wall Street for McCombs as a leadership program, not an internship training club. When we identify students, we look for the ones who will become successful alumni and give back to UT. Interviews for junior summer internships are happening earlier and earlier, starting now in November of sophomore year. The timeline can be penalizing for later bloomers, but we've just had to adapt to the reality of the marketplace and have shifted our admissions timeline from October to September. The freshman-year investment banking clubs are helpful, since they train students who eventually enter my program and sit for early interviews. Landing the internship is only half the battle — the other half is getting the return offer , so we spend a lot of time coaching kids to succeed at their summer jobs. We really focus on the fundamentals and technical skills, which are still important on the job, even with AI . They still have to understand the concepts of building a model, since they can't sit in a board meeting and open ChatGPT. We run a banking simulation during the course, where students create a pitchbook for a real corporate client, like Nike or Pepsi. The project trains them to work in a team and with a client, and getting practice with the grunt work helps them hit the ground running at their summer internships. The winning teams present to the client, usually to the company's CFO. The alumni base is incredibly engaged, and they make it a mission to hire more Longhorns. Alumni take ownership of a student every year, coaching them through the process, and ultimately try to grow the UT presence at their firms. Unfortunately, it's a changing world, and a lot of schools are mimicking our model, so we've had to step up our game to make sure UT students still excel. The secret sauce is in the execution and finesse. Succeeding when there We have a nearly 100% return-offer rate, and placement is a big part of why. We've built strong relationships with the firms, and I know where students will thrive. Investment banks are like people, with different personalities and needs . It's about optimizing for cultural fit. Beyond being well-prepared, UT students are uniquely humble. They're very collaborative, and the banks love that — I've even seen groups of students preparing for the same interview together. My program has become a positive feedback loop: the more students we place in New York, the more people want to come to UT, which makes the student body even stronger and helps us place more people. items.title: Inside Meta's grind to turn Muse from a clunky chatbot into an AI sensation
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hypes up its Muse AI assistant at the company's Connect event. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu Meta's top AI staff fretted about Muse days before launch as it struggled to speak good English. Ex-GitHub CEO Nat Friedman's team worked around the clock to turn the AI assistant into a hit. After a "long ass" grind, Muse is now a "banger," says Meta's 29-year-old AI chief, Alexandr Wang. A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products. Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger." Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider. Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup. Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale. For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago. "Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said. Nat Friedman grinds to turn Muse into a hit Muse's success was far from inevitable. Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch." As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests. Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added. Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort. That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it. The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before. "Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect. Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor. Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies." He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel. When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch. He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent. While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said. Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted. Meta goes on an AI hiring spree Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team. Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X. The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before. Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant. More to come after Muse Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction. "We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note. Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes. "They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said. At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote. Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath. For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse. "The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X. Have a tip? items.title: We asked our Gen Z and millennial reporters and editors about AI agents. Here's where they split.
items.summary: Members of Business Insider's economy team chat about their thoughts on AI agents. Bartie Scott/Business Insider I spoke with my colleagues at Business Insider to hear their thoughts on AI agents. Opinions varied. Millennials on the team were cautiously optimistic, seeing potential for efficiency in daily tasks. Gen Zers seemed skeptical and worried about privacy concerns and scams. Everyone is talking about AI agents — and Business Insider's reporters and editors are no different. Agents go a step beyond chatbots and are capable of planning and achieving multi-step tasks. This can range from making a restaurant reservation to inviting a friend for lunch to buying clothes you are on the lookout for. To get a sense of how members of different generations feel about the emerging world of AI agents, I, a Gen Z fellow on the Business Insider Economy team, talked to my colleagues, spanning from Gen Z to elder millennials, about their stances on the divisive topic. While the younger generation expressed a lot of worries around privacy, the millennials in the group were cautiously optimistic about how agents could be helpful at work and at home. The Gen Z consensus: Skepticism and privacy concerns Many of my Gen Z peers agreed that growing up with technology made them more aware of its limitations and dangers — making them more hesitant about handing over their information to AI agents. They also seemed most concerned about privacy and scams. The younger members of the Economy team aren't alone — a recent poll from the Pew Research Center found that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of AI's benefits . Ayelet Sheffey, our Gen Z senior education reporter, said she was not open to handing over the control to an AI agent to get things she needed done. "I'm hearing about people using AI and they're like feeding their bank information or personal things into a software — that just immediately turns me off," she said. "Not only for the privacy reasons, but also, I just don't trust anyone or anything else to get tasks done." Allie Kelly, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while being a reporter is a public-facing job, there is other information she prefers to keep private. While she is open to using it for professional purposes, she is more hesitant to use it for personal reasons, not knowing how the information she provides to the agent can be used. "If I want an agent to analyze something, I will give it something specific to analyze — I'm not going to give it access to my inbox," she said. "It's not just my information; sometimes it's sources' information, so I just want to be cognizant of that." Juliana Kaplan, a Gen Z senior reporter, said she is wary of handing her personal information over to companies that could have different incentives influencing how their AI agents work. She posed a rhetorical question: If a company with an AI agent had a deal with a credit card company, and she was using an agent to choose her next credit card, would it be influenced to recommend that one? "I would have to do a lot of research into the amount of due diligence they have done with my information," she said. "At that point, I'm like, I can just do it myself." Noah Sheidlower, a Gen Z senior economy reporter, said, "I'm all for efficiency and maximizing time I could be spending on things that are meaningful to me, but I don't fully trust giving up my authority and agency to make decisions. I've read stories of agents invading privacy and doing tasks it should not be doing that have harmful repercussions, and I want to stay in control as much as I can until the agents are more advanced." Madison Hoff, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while she sees the value of agents in helping manage work, she enjoys working on things herself. When looking for craft ideas in her free time, she said she enjoys the process of looking around her and finding ideas — even if an AI agent would help her do it more quickly. "I rather just use the brain power a little more and do the research," she said. Several of the Gen Z reporters said that while friends in creative fields were more hesitant to adopt AI agents, peers in finance, consulting, and tech-adjacent fields seemed more open to adopting them earlier. The millennial consensus: Cautious optimism The idea that AI agents still have a long way to go before they are accurate and efficient enough was shared by the Economy team's millennial editors, who held a more cautious optimism about the future of adopting agents to streamline workflows and team operations. Bartie Scott, a millennial and economy deputy editor, said that while she has environmental concerns about using AI, she does see potential in using it to reduce her screen time — especially with voice agents . "As someone who has a job that's on a screen, it can feel insurmountable sometimes," she said. "We have so much to do in modern life that you feel burned out — And I think this, maybe in an ideal world, could be like a solution to that." Scott said that while she is not an early adopter of technology, once she has seen people she respects say the technology is trustworthy and easy to use, she might be inclined to dabble in it. Examples she thought of would be if she could get an agent to help brief her on her workday priorities and daily check-ins. "If I could do all that with voice commands, that would kind of be a dream," she said. Andy Kiersz, a millennial and senior economic data editor, agreed that he might be more in the mid-adopter camp than the early-adopter camp. If a "sufficiently long period of time" passes with no major data breaches and a situation like planning a trip arises where it would be useful, he said he would consider using an agent. Kiersz sees some potential for agentic AI at work. "I could totally see putting an agent to go crawl repositories of economics papers and read through the abstracts," he said. He sees himself sending agents to do the "tedious side of the job," so he can focus on the "interesting side of the job." Two millennials on the team had the most hands-on experience with these new toys. Ryan Kailath, an elder millennial and senior editor, is a "big pointsmaxxer," as a member of many airline loyalty programs . Yet, finding awards when booking is always a hefty logistical task. So Kailath used Muse , the personal AI agent launched by Meta in early September, to see what all the fuss was about and look into booking for an upcoming trip. Although the AI agent took the lead, it encountered many problems that Kailath had to resolve manually, such as login credentials and two-factor authentication codes required to continue the search. "My one test case where I thought, 'Here's a big friction in my life, maybe an agent could make this friction easier,' it failed miserably," he said. Yet, Kailath said that if it improved in the future, he would no doubt use it. Our Senior Reporter, Jacob Zinkula, also had a brief 10-minute encounter with Muse . Zinkula, a young millennial, downloaded the app to see if it could help him get a future reservation at a high-demand restaurant for the Christmas season, but has yet to figure it out. Caught in the cusp of the Gen Z and millennial generations, he is more cautious about letting an AI agent make financial decisions on its own, but is open to waiting to see how they could develop and be useful in the future. "I try to be open but skeptical," he said. "It doesn't feel like there's an immediate need for me to like jump onto it too soon. That said, I'm open to ways it could be helpful going forward. For better or worse, this stuff's probably not going away." Read the original article on Business Insider
